chunks: Abu Ali Al-Ash'ari, from Muhammad ibn Abd al-Jabbar, from Safwan, from Abu al-Fadl Salim al-Hannat, who said:

Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) said to me: 'What is your trade?' I said, 'I am a wheat merchant (Hannat). Sometimes I arrive when there is a market surplus (nafaq), and sometimes I arrive when there is a market slump (kasad), so I withhold it.' He (peace be upon him) said: 'So what do those in front of you say about it?' I said, 'They say,

key_terms.حَكَمُ بْنُ حِزَام: A companion of the Prophet known for his wealth and trade
key_terms.حَنَّاط: Wheat merchant (one who buys and sells wheat)
key_terms.مُحْتَكِر: Monopolizer / One who hoards goods to raise prices
key_terms.نَفَاق: Market surplus or abundance of goods

ai.seo_question: What is the difference between general hoarding and the prohibited monopoly (ihtikar) in Shia jurisprudence?
ai.summary: This hadith from *Al-Kafi* clarifies the nuanced Shia jurisprudence on *ihtikar* (hoarding), distinguishing between general market holding and strategic monopoly. Imam al-Sadiq (AS) references the Prophet’s warning to Hakim ibn Hizam, a prominent Qurayshi merchant known for buying up all incoming food supplies, to illustrate that the prohibition targets those who control the total supply to manipulate prices, rather than ordinary merchants holding small portions. This distinction underscores the practical implication that moderate inventory management is permissible, provided it does not constitute a monopoly that harms the public interest.
